name: Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency (SAMA; since 2020 the Saudi Central Bank)

summary.text: The Saudi Arabian Monetary Agency (SAMA), renamed the Saudi Central Bank in November 2020, is the kingdom's central bank and holds its official foreign assets. On July 9, 1974, before Treasury Secretary William Simon's trip to Jidda, Simon told President Nixon he wanted a Saudi commitment to buy long- and short-term U.S. securities. GAO reported in 1979 that the Treasury's noncompetitive 'add-on' facility for buying Treasuries outside the auctions was first offered to Saudi Arabia, and that former Treasury officials said country-level data were withheld because of confidentiality commitments to Saudi Arabia. The Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation (communique of June 8, 1974) was co-chaired by the Treasury Secretary and funded from a Saudi trust account at the Treasury. In May 2016 the Treasury published Saudi holdings of Treasuries ($116.8 billion) separately for the first time, after a Bloomberg FOIA request.

facts.claim: On July 9, 1974, before Treasury Secretary William Simon's trip to the Middle East, President Nixon told Simon he had raised oil prices privately with King Faisal. Simon said he wanted a commitment from the Saudis to purchase long- and short-term U.S. securities, which he described as helpful for U.S. money markets. The conversation is printed as Document 360 of the FRUS Energy Crisis volume.
facts.quote: I want some commitment from them to purchase of long- and short-term securities, which would be very helpful for our money markets.

sources.title: Memorandum of Conversation, Nixon and William Simon, July 9, 1974 (NSA Memoranda of Conversation)

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXXVI, Energy Crisis 1969-1974, Document 360: Memorandum of Conversation (Nixon, Simon, Scowcroft), July 9, 1974

facts.claim: A FRUS editorial note records that Simon left for the Middle East and Europe on July 11, 1974 to promote a reduction in oil prices, and that Nixon told him the effort to get prices down must be done very privately.
facts.quote: On July 11, 1974, Secretary of the Treasury William Simon traveled to the Middle East and Europe to promote the reduction of oil prices.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXVII, Iran; Iraq 1973-1976, Document 65: Editorial Note (Simon's July 1974 trip)

facts.claim: On July 30, 1974, after his return, Simon told Nixon that the United States would certainly get Arab investment in the U.S. Treasury, that Kuwait would also invest and Indonesia already was, and that Saudi Arabia would help but did not want to bear the whole burden.
facts.quote: we will get Arab investment in the U.S. Treasury certainly. Kuwait will also and Indonesia is.

sources.title: Memorandum of Conversation, Nixon and William Simon, July 30, 1974 (NSA Memoranda of Conversation)

facts.claim: The General Accounting Office reported in June 1979 that the Treasury's noncompetitive 'add-on' facility, under which a buyer purchases Treasury securities outside the competitive auction, was first offered to Saudi Arabia and had since been made available to all governments and central banks.
facts.quote: The noncompetitive 'add-on' purchase facility for Treasury securities was first offered to Saudi Arabia, and it is now available to all governments and central banks.

sources.title: Are OPEC Financial Holdings a Danger to U.S. Banks or the Economy? (EMD-79-45)

facts.claim: The same 1979 GAO report stated that former Treasury officials said country-specific information on OPEC holdings was held confidentially not for statistical or legal reasons but because the Treasury had made special commitments of financial confidentiality to Saudi Arabia and perhaps other OPEC governments. GAO concluded that limiting publication of these data afforded special privileges to OPEC nations and recommended that Treasury and Commerce justify them to Congress.
facts.quote: access to data concerning OPEC holdings in the United States exists, but publication of this information to Congress and the public is limited, thus affording special privileges to OPEC nations.

sources.title: Are OPEC Financial Holdings a Danger to U.S. Banks or the Economy? (EMD-79-45)
OPEC Financial Holdings in the United States (testimony of J. Dexter Peach, July 16, 1979)

facts.claim: In July 1979 testimony, GAO said information on OPEC deposits and loans in U.S. banks by country had been confidential, that the Treasury's $12.4 billion figure for OPEC purchases of U.S. government securities covered all OPEC holdings of U.S. debt instruments, and that a possible liquidation of those holdings would disrupt U.S. financial markets only temporarily.
facts.quote: the possible liquidation by OPEC nations of their deposits in U.S. banks and their holdings of U.S. Government securities would disrupt U.S. financial markets only temporarily.

sources.title: OPEC Financial Holdings in the United States (testimony of J. Dexter Peach, July 16, 1979)

facts.claim: In an April 1975 airgram, U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia James Akins wrote that Saudi Arabia had already agreed that year to place enough funds in Treasury notes and FNMA issues to cover more than half of the U.S. balance-of-payments deficit, which he treated as a sign of friendship.
facts.quote: Saudi Arabia has already agreed this year to place enough in Treasury notes and FNMA issues to cover more than half our balance of payment deficit.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of State, Office of the Historian
sources.title: FRUS 1969-1976, vol. XXXVII, Energy Crisis 1974-1980, Document 52: Airgram From the Ambassador to Saudi Arabia (Akins)

facts.claim: Bloomberg's May 30, 2016 feature, based on documents obtained from the National Archives and a FOIA request, reported that the 1974 arrangement let Saudi Arabia bypass the competitive bidding process through 'add-ons' excluded from official auction totals, that King Faisal demanded the purchases stay strictly secret, and that the Treasury reported the holdings only within a regional grouping.
facts.quote: the U.S. allowed Saudi Arabia to bypass the normal competitive bidding process for buying Treasuries by creating 'add-ons.' Those sales, which were excluded from the official auction totals, hid all traces of Saudi Arabia's presence in the U.S. government debt market.

sources.publisher: Bloomberg (Andrea Wong), syndicated in the Austin American-Statesman
sources.title: The untold story behind Saudi Arabia's 41-year U.S. debt secret

sources.publisher: Bloomberg (Andrea Wong), reprinted by Energy Voice

facts.claim: The same Bloomberg feature reported that Gerald Parsky, Simon's deputy on the 1974 trip, said the secret arrangement should have been dismantled years earlier and that he was surprised the Treasury kept it in place for so long.
facts.quote: Parsky says the secret arrangement with the Saudis should have been dismantled years ago and was surprised the Treasury kept it in place for so long.

sources.publisher: Bloomberg (Andrea Wong), reprinted by Energy Voice

facts.claim: On May 16, 2016 the U.S. Treasury, responding to a Bloomberg FOIA request, published Saudi Arabia's holdings of Treasury securities separately for the first time: $116.8 billion as of March 2016, ranking 13th among foreign holders. Since 1974 the holdings had been reported only within an 'oil exporters' grouping. A Treasury spokesperson said the decision was not linked to Saudi warnings about selling U.S. assets over 9/11 litigation legislation.
facts.quote: Saudi Arabia held $116.8 billion in U.S. Treasury debt, and this was the first time the department had broken out the kingdom's figure.

Saudi Arabia holds $117B in US debt: Report
Saudi Arabia's 41-year secret is out: US Treasuries total $116.8 billion

facts.claim: In November 2020 King Salman approved the Saudi Central Bank Law, which renamed the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority the Saudi Central Bank, reporting directly to the King, with the new bank taking over the former agency's rights and obligations and keeping the SAMA acronym. The law sets three objectives: monetary stability, financial-sector stability and support for economic growth.
facts.quote: the Saudi Central Bank shall replace the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority in its rights and obligations, and wherever the name appears in related laws, regulations, orders, and decisions.

sources.title: News release on the Saudi Central Bank Law
Issuance of the new Saudi Central Bank Law

facts.claim: David Spiro's 1999 Cornell University Press study of petrodollar recycling argues that most of the 1970s oil surplus was not recycled by markets to deficit countries, and that the United States made a deal with Saudi Arabia to sell it U.S. securities in secret, resulting in a substantial portion of Saudi assets being held by the U.S. government.
facts.quote: the United States made a deal with Saudi Arabia to sell it U.S. securities in secret, a deal resulting in a substantial portion of Saudi assets being held by the U.S. government.

sources.title: David E. Spiro, The Hidden Hand of American Hegemony: Petrodollar Recycling and International Markets

facts.claim: The U.S.-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation was formally set up in June 1974 under a joint communique of June 8, 1974 signed by Secretary of State Kissinger and Prince Fahd. GAO reported in March 1979 that it was co-chaired by the U.S. Treasury Secretary and the Saudi Minister of Finance and National Economy, that U.S. technical assistance was funded almost entirely from the Saudi Arabian Trust Account in the U.S. Treasury, and that as of September 1978 sixteen project agreements worth about $800 million were under way.
facts.quote: U.S. technical assistance is funded almost entirely from the Saudi Arabian Trust Account in the U.S. Treasury.

facts.claim: In March 1974 the State Department instructed the embassy in Jidda to approach the Saudis promptly at a high level, suggesting Prince Fahd, to discuss joint commissions for closer cooperation in economic, military/strategic and scientific fields, as an alternative to European arrangements exchanging technology for guaranteed oil supply. The embassy replied that the Saudi reaction was uniformly enthusiastic and that the Saudis insisted the matter be kept secret until announced simultaneously in Washington and Riyadh.
facts.quote: the Saudis also insisted that the matter be kept secret until officially announced simultaneously in Washington and Riyadh.

connections.quote: The noncompetitive 'add-on' purchase facility for Treasury securities was first offered to Saudi Arabia, and it is now available to all governments and central banks.

connections.claim: SAMA is the central bank of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia; the 2020 Saudi Central Bank Law places it in direct reporting to the King.
connections.quote: the new law changing the name of the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority to the Saudi Central Bank, with direct reporting to the King.

openQuestions: The widely repeated claim of a 1974 U.S.-Saudi pact under which Saudi Arabia agreed to price oil only in dollars in exchange for U.S. protection is not supported by any document found here. The primary records reviewed (FRUS vol. XXXVI Doc. 360, the Ford Library memcons of July 9 and 30, 1974, GAO EMD-79-45 and ID-79-7, FRUS vol. XXXVII Doc. 52) describe Saudi purchases of U.S. securities, a confidential add-on facility, and a technical-cooperation commission; none states a dollar-invoicing obligation or a protection-for-pricing exchange. Radio Free Asia's July 2024 fact check found no known formal deal requiring Saudi oil sales in dollars (https://www.rfa.org/english/news/afcl/afcl-us-saudi-oil-deal-07082024043619.html). Whether an unwritten understanding existed is not settled by the public record and should be recorded as unsupported, not refuted.

The original Bloomberg feature of May 30, 2016 (bloomberg.com/news/features/2016-05-30/...) was not returned by search; the feature is cited here through its syndicated reprints (Austin American-Statesman, Energy Voice). The owner should check the quotes against the Bloomberg original. Simon's congressional testimony that 'regional reporting' was the only way Saudi Arabia would agree to invest through the add-on system is reported only in that feature; the hearing record was not located.

No 1974 Treasury document creating the add-on arrangement itself was found; the earliest government description located is GAO's June 1979 report EMD-79-45. The FRUS vol. XXXVII volume was not searched document by document, and it may contain the Jidda telegrams on the SAMA commitment.

The July 9, 1974 quote ('helpful for our money markets') is from the Ford Library scan; the FRUS Document 360 excerpt returned by search paraphrases the same passage as a commitment 'to put their funds in long and short term securities'. The wording should be confirmed against the FRUS page.

Treasury's 2016 release followed decades of reporting Saudi holdings within an aggregate; GAO's 1979 report says the add-on facility later became available to all governments and central banks, so the confidentiality of the Saudi line rather than the facility itself is what remained exceptional. The recurring-cast GAP 1954-1977 box asks for a mechanism linking the consortium era to Gulf sovereign money: the record found here documents petrodollar recycling into Treasuries (1974-75) and the Joint Commission (1974), but no document links the 1954 Iranian consortium's beneficiaries to these Saudi arrangements.
Sources differ on the English rendering of the pre-2020 name ('Agency' vs 'Authority'); SAMA's own 2020 release uses 'Authority'.
